passage: Hansa, you came home quiet today. Did someone ask you again where you're "really" from? Sit with your Disha nani. When I was fifteen, my family moved from Imphal to Delhi. On the first day a teacher said, "Your Hindi is so good!" I smiled. The next day a girl asked, "But where are you really from?" I said Imphal. "No, originally?" I said Imphal again. In the market a shopkeeper spoke to me slowly, as if I couldn't understand. Each time it was small, a sting like an ant bite. But by the end of the month I felt I had a hundred bites. I stopped raising my hand. I thought, whatever I do, they'll see me as the girl from somewhere else. It was my friend Rukmini who just asked me what music I liked. That was the first day in Delhi I felt like a person, not a place.

qa.a: She probably thought it was harmless curiosity, not realising that repeating it made Disha feel she didn't belong.

passage: Results day at the private school in Nagpur was chaos: rain hammering the tin shed, parents crowding the notice board, the printer jammed. Suraj, fifteen, the scholarship student from the municipal colony, pushed through to find his name: first in science. A teacher patted his shoulder. "Wow, Suraj! So smart, for someone from your background." A parent nearby said, "Scholarship boy? Really?" Suraj smiled politely. It was the third time that week. On Monday, someone had asked if his father "worked here" when he came to drop him. On Wednesday, a classmate had been surprised he spoke good English. Each comment was small. But standing under the dripping shed, holding his result, Suraj felt oddly alone. His friend Ujjwal nudged him. "First! Treat!" Suraj laughed, but the word "background" kept ringing in his ears.

passage: Dilnaz, sixteen, had moved from Srinagar to Pune two years ago. On Monday, in the canteen queue, a senior said, "Your English is really good. Did you learn it here?" passage: In the Madrid school canteen, Pablo, fifteen, sat across from Elif, who'd moved from Istanbul last year. She'd just aced the history test. "You're so clever," he said, grinning. "Honestly, you don't seem Turkish at all. You're really modern." He meant it kindly. He'd heard his uncle say similar things about his Turkish colleagues. Elif's smile froze. She put down her fork. "What does that mean? Turkish people aren't modern?" Pablo blinked. "No, I just meant... it was a compliment." "It didn't feel like one," she said quietly and went to sit with her friends. Pablo sat there, stunned. He'd only wanted to be nice. That night he replayed the words and heard them the way Elif had. His face burned. The compliment had carried an insult inside it.

passage: I remember the moment clearly, even two years later. It was my first term at the Delhi college. In the corridor, a senior said loudly, "Madrasi girl, bring us some idli tomorrow," and his friends laughed. I'm from Coimbatore, and I'm not a "Madrasi," and nobody there calls us that. I froze. Part of me wanted to say, "Please don't call me that." Part of me thought, am I overreacting? It's just a joke. Will they make my life hard if I speak? I said nothing and walked on. That night I told Imran, my classmate, and he said, "You don't have to fight every battle. But you don't have to swallow it either." I didn't sleep much. A week later, when it happened again, I said calmly, "My name's Kavitha." They stopped. Both choices were mine. Carrying the silence had been heavier.

qa.a: He called her "Madrasi girl."

qa.a: Kavitha felt hurt and unsure, torn between speaking up and worrying about overreacting or causing trouble.

qa.a: That staying silent or speaking up are both valid choices, and that she didn't have to swallow the hurt every time.

Mridul (third-year, marketing intern) came to see me after the team lunch. A senior manager had said to him, "You people from small towns are very hardworking, not like the city kids." passage:
Tuesday night
In tutorial today Naveen said, "For a girl from a small town, you're really confident." Everyone smiled like it was a nice thing. I smiled too. Now I'm lying here thinking about it.
Was it nice? Or did he mean small-town girls are usually scared? Am I making it bigger than it is?
If I say something tomorrow, he'll say "I was praising you," and I'll look touchy. If I don't, it just sits in my stomach with all the other little ones.
I think I'll ask him, lightly, "What did you mean about small-town girls?" If he meant well, fine. If not, at least he'll think.
Either way, I'm allowed to be tired of it.
- Elizabeth
